name: Rafael Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There isn't really a normal one. I lead a storm restoration crew for Brightline, a contractor that power companies hire when the weather wrecks their lines. When it's quiet, we do planned rebuild work near home, swapping old poles. When a big storm hits somewhere, we load four trucks and drive, sometimes ten hours, and then it's sixteen-hour days for two weeks, sleeping in school gyms. I love the moment a whole street gets its lights back and people come out and clap. What wears me out is not knowing if I'll be home on Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how does money look?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ana, my partner, is a dental hygienist. We're getting married next September, and we're saving for a flat at the same time, which is not a smart combination. We've got about four months of savings. The storm money is good, but it comes in lumps, so some months are fat and some are thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, nothing radical. I can picture that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, useful for small things. I use it now and then to plan the drive to a storm or check a hotel. With the crew I wouldn't talk about it much, we'd be talking about the next storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's the same worries as now. Brightline lost the eastern contract last spring and four crews got let go, so the real risk is contracts, not computers. A contractor lineman is only as safe as the next contract, and no robot decides that, a purchasing manager does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep my head down, and keep my certificates current so I'm one of the crews they keep. I'd put the storm bonuses straight into the flat fund and keep the wedding modest, maybe seventy guests instead of a hundred and twenty. I'd also keep an eye on jobs at the public utility, which pay a bit less but don't lose contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's the usual uneasy. It's not AI, it's being a contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said seventy guests instead of a hundred and twenty. Has that conversation happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. Ana's family is big, and her mum has a list. I'd say we put the money into the flat instead, and her mum would give me a look across the table that I'd remember for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move to the public utility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If another contract went, yes. Less storm money, but a steady wage and a pension. With a flat and a wedding, steady starts to look good.

say: I'd say AI turned out **useful for small things**, like planning drives.
With the crew I'd talk about **the next storm**, not AI.
think: The real risk is **lost contracts**, like the eastern one last spring.
A **purchasing manager**, not a robot, decides my job.
do: Keep **certificates current** to stay among the crews kept.
Put **storm bonuses** into the flat fund and trim the wedding.
Watch for openings at the **public utility**.
feel: **Uneasy** in the usual way that comes with contract work.
S0.quote: A contractor lineman is only as safe as the next contract, and no robot decides that, a purchasing manager does.
fieldNote: His worry predates AI: **contract churn** already cost four crews their jobs.
**Lumpy storm pay** plus a wedding and a flat squeeze his cushion.
He weighs **steady public pay** against bigger contractor bonuses.

steps.text: Keep all line and first aid certificates current
Put every storm bonus into the flat fund
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 70
Watch for openings at the public utility

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, the office stuff changes. Contractors would feel that, because so much of the bidding is paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is changing the paperwork, not the poles. At Brightline I'd say we should use it to get to storms faster than other contractors, because speed wins contracts. To friends I'd say I'm fine for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's mixed for me. If AI plans storm logistics better, the power companies need fewer contractor crews standing by. On the other hand, storms are getting worse, so there's more work. I'd probably come out okay, but the guys on weaker crews might not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the routing and logistics tools properly once the other leads showed me they work, maybe in the first six months. I'd do the company's course on the new job-pack software. I'd still go ahead with the wedding and the flat, just with a slightly bigger cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit more than now, but no panic. Most of my job is still a pole, a truck and sixteen hours in the rain, and software doesn't change that part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the weaker crews you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones without a good lead, or with older trucks. When the power company picks who stays for the second week, they pick the crews that finished fastest. If AI makes speed easier to measure, the slow ones go home first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything with the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd keep the date. I'd just want five months saved instead of four before we sign for a flat. Ana agrees with me on that one, which is rare.

say: I'd say AI changes the **paperwork**, not the **poles**.
I'd push Brightline to use AI to **reach storms faster**.
think: Better planning could mean **fewer standby crews**, but storms bring more work.
**Slower crews** would feel it first, not mine.
do: Use **routing tools** once other leads prove they work.
Take the company course on **job-pack software**.
Keep the wedding date but save **five months** before buying.
feel: **Uneasy**, a bit more than now, but no panic.
S1.quote: Most of my job is still a pole, a truck and sixteen hours in the rain, and software doesn't change that part.
fieldNote: He sees AI as a **competitive edge** for contractors that move first.
He expects **speed metrics** to decide which crews keep work.
His steady style shows: adopt **after peers** prove it.

steps.text: Start using the routing tools after other leads test them
Build savings to five months before signing for a flat
Keep the September wedding date with Ana

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 and 2031. The office side of Brightline goes first, then us. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to know what Brightline's plan is, now, not in 2030. To friends I'd say I've got a few years and I'll be fine, because nobody wants to hear a groom panicking. I'd keep off social media, it'd be full of nonsense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Contractors go first. When robots can do the work, power companies won't pay a contractor to drive four trucks ten hours; they'll send a robot from the nearest depot. So I think my storm work shrinks even before 2031, maybe as soon as the planning goes AI in 2028. Ana's job is hands-on in people's mouths, so she might keep hers a bit longer, but dentists cut costs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone the flat, honestly, and keep renting. The wedding would go ahead but small, at her parents' garden. In the first year I'd apply to the public utility to get inside before contractors are dropped, and I'd ask about training on robot crews while I'm there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be a groom in September and out of storm work by 2030, and I'd be smiling in the photos anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would contract work go before the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the planning AI would squeeze everything. It'd tell the power company exactly how many crews to call and for how long, and the answer would always be fewer, for shorter. We make our money on the long second week, and that'd go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, the same night. We decided before the engagement that money talk happens at the kitchen table, not in bits. I'd say we keep her job steady, I move to the utility, and the flat waits two years.

say: I'd ask Brightline for **its plan now**, not in 2030.
I'd tell friends **I'll be fine**, because nobody wants a panicking groom.
think: **Contractors go first**, as planning AI squeezes storm callouts from 2028.
Ana's **hands-on job** may last longer, though dentists cut costs too.
do: Hold a **small wedding** at her parents' garden.
Apply to the **public utility** in the first year.
feel: **Alarmed**, expecting to lose storm work around his wedding.
S2.quote: I'd be a groom in September and out of storm work by 2030, and I'd be smiling in the photos anyway.
fieldNote: He sees AI planning cutting the **second storm week** where contractors earn most.
His public calm hides a **private alarm**, a clear say-think gap.
He and Ana share **kitchen-table** money talks, a source of steadiness.

steps.text: Postpone buying a flat and keep renting
Apply for a lineman job at the public utility
Hold a small wedding in Ana's parents' garden
Ask the utility about training on robot crews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. So we'd be married, maybe in the flat, before anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, and the smart thing is to move into the public utility before the rush. At Brightline I'd be honest with the crew that I'm looking around. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to get into a safer job and probably buy the flat first. The storm logistics change by 2031, so the contractor money would start drying up then. I'd be thirty-five when robots arrive, still young enough for something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the public utility in the next two years, while they're still hiring. I'd keep the wedding as planned, maybe a hundred guests, and buy the flat in 2028 on the utility salary. I'd start learning the robot supervision side once the utility runs trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but managing. Five years is enough time to swap storm bonuses for a pension before the storms stop needing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't you miss the storms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. People clapping in the street when the lights come on, you don't get that at a depot. But I'd rather miss it than be the last contractor standing in a gym waiting for a call that doesn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do that you wouldn't in the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat. In the fast one I'd wait. With five years I'd buy, because a few years of payments while I'm still earning is better than renting forever.

say: I'd say the smart move is joining the **public utility** before the rush.
I'd be **honest with the crew** that I'm looking around.
think: Five years gives time to switch and **buy the flat** first.
Contractor money **dries up from 2031**, with robots when I'm thirty-five.
do: Move to the **public utility** within two years.
Buy the flat in **2028** on the utility salary.
Learn **robot supervision** once the utility runs trials.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to swap storm bonuses for a pension before the storms stop needing me.
fieldNote: Five years changes the **flat decision**: buy now rather than wait.
He'd **trade storm thrills** for a pension, though he'd miss them.
His pragmatism shows in a clear, **dated plan**.

steps.text: Move to the public utility within two years
Buy a flat in 2028 on the utility wage
Join the utility's robot supervision trials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, 2039 for robots. I'd be thirty-nine or forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long way off, and I'd get on with the storms. To friends I'd say this is the version where we all have time. I might mention it at the wedding speech, as a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I could do storm work for six or seven more years, save the bonuses, and still move to the utility in my early thirties. The thinking side, the planning and contracts, changes in 2036. It's a slow fade, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing storm work, save hard, buy the flat in 2028. Move to the utility around 2032 and get into the robot programme there. Maybe think about a kid around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly fine. It's on my mind the way my pension is, something for later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wedding joke be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like, Ana married a lineman, but by our tenth anniversary she'll be married to a man who tells robots where to climb. Her uncle would laugh, her mum wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk in waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that everyone waits. If every contractor lineman tries to get into the utility in 2033, there won't be room. The best time to leave a contractor is a few years before everyone else realises they should.

say: I'd say it's **a long way off** and get on with storms.
I'd tell friends this is the version where **we all have time**.
think: I could do storm work for **six or seven** more years.
It feels like **a slow fade**, not a cliff.
do: Keep doing **storm work** and save the bonuses.
Move to the utility around **2032** and join its robot programme.
feel: **Uneasy**, a little, like a pension he'll think about later.
S4.quote: The best time to leave a contractor is a few years before everyone else realises they should.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **bank storm bonuses** before switching.
He sees the risk of **everyone waiting** and crowding the utility.
Family plans, including **a child around 2030**, go ahead.

steps.text: Keep leading the storm crew and bank the bonuses
Buy a flat with Ana in 2028
Move to the public utility around 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because contractors would be the first thing the power companies cut and I'd be newly married. What would help is the public utilities agreeing to take experienced contractor linemen first when they start robot programmes. Someone who has rebuilt a town after an ice storm should be first in line to teach the robots, not last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the storms themselves. They're getting worse every year. If robots come, I just hope they come in enough numbers, because the night a whole region goes dark, nobody cares who climbs the pole as long as somebody does.

headlineQuote: Someone who has rebuilt a town after an ice storm should be first in line to teach the robots, not last.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old storm crew lead** for a contractor that power companies hire after bad weather.
He is **marrying Ana**, a dental hygienist, next September and saving for a flat at the same time.
His existing worry is **contract churn**, so he is uneasy even when AI changes little.
He uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools after other crew leads prove them.
As warning time grows he moves from **alarm** to a **dated plan** to join the public utility.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because contractor crews would be cut first just as he marries.
whatWouldHelp: Public utilities hiring **experienced contractor linemen first** for robot programmes.
